name: Saterland Frisian

ancestors.notes: Descent from Old Frisian (East Frisian branch). Saterland Frisian is the last surviving dialect of East Frisian, spoken in the Saterland (Seelterland) municipalities since medieval Frisian colonisation of the bogs.
Low German adstrate: Saterland is surrounded by Low German speakers. Heavy Low German influence on lexicon and some phonological convergence, especially in younger speakers.
Standard German adstrate: dominant language of education and administration. All Saterland Frisians are trilingual (Saterland Frisian, Low German, Standard German).
Dutch adstrate: historical trade contacts with the Netherlands; some Dutch-influenced lexical items, particularly in older vocabulary.

notes: Saterland Frisian (Seeltersk) — the last surviving variety of East Frisian, spoken by ~1,000–2,500 people in the four Saterland municipalities (Ramsloh, Strücklingen, Scharrel, Sedelsberg) in the Cloppenburg district of Lower Saxony, Germany. Severely endangered; recognised as a minority language under the European Charter. KEY FEATURES, per Peters (2017), the JIPA illustration: (1) MOST CONSERVATIVE FRISIAN: preserves features lost in West and North Frisian. (2) NO CENTRING DIPHTHONGS. Peters (2017) lists exactly seven phonemic diphthongs, /oi̯ ɛi̯ œi̯ ɔi̯ ai̯ ɔu̯ au̯/, all falling and closing; there is no /iə oə uə/ series. An earlier revision of this spec carried centring diphthongs for the ⟨oa/ia/ua⟩ digraphs, apparently copied from West Frisian's ⟨ea/oa⟩ pattern (`fy.json`) — that is contradicted both by Peters and by the wikipron gold, where every one of 73 ⟨oa⟩ tokens transcribes as the long monophthong /ɔː/ and ⟨ia/ua⟩ are effectively unattested. (3) FINAL DEVOICING of lenis obstruents, as in continental West Germanic generally. (4) /ɡ/ IS PHONEMICALLY A VOICED VELAR STOP for Peters's consultants, but 'some older speakers realize /ɡ/ as a velar fricative [ɣ], which is voiced in all positions except before voiceless consonants and word-finally' (Peters 2017: 224); the wikipron gold's spelling pronunciations use the fricative variant essentially throughout (80/80 realised /ɡ/ tokens are [ɣ]), so both values are kept as candidates. (5) /sp, st/ → [ʃp, ʃt] word-initially (shared with Low German). (6) /s/ becomes voiced word-medially before /j/, after /l, r/, and intervocalically after a long vowel (Peters 2017: 224). (7) RICH FRONT ROUNDED VOWELS: ö/öö, ü/üü from i-umlaut; /yː/ is largely restricted to Low German loans. (8) Long ää /ɛː/ preserved as distinct from ee /eː/, matching Peters's long lax vs. long tense mid-vowel contrast. (9) OPEN-SYLLABLE VOWEL LENGTH: the gold follows Fort's (2015) orthographic convention (also adopted by Peters 2017), under which a long vowel in an open syllable is spelled with a SINGLE vowel letter, not a doubled one (Kramer's 1961/1982 dictionary convention instead doubles every long vowel). ⟨Apel⟩ 'apple' /aːpəl/ vs. ⟨Adder⟩ 'snake' /adər/ is the minimal contrast this reflects; it is why the spec keys plain a/i/o/u to `open_syllable` rather than trying to fold length onto the letters themselves. (10) THREE-LANGUAGE ecology: all speakers also speak Low German and Standard German.
